subject: biology
title: Immunology basics
summary: How the innate and adaptive immune systems detect and destroy pathogens, how antigens are presented to T cells, what B cells, T cells and antibodies do, how immunological memory forms and why vaccines work.
body:
The immune system is the collection of cells, tissues and molecules that protects the body from pathogens and abnormal cells. It has two connected branches: a fast, general first response and a slower, highly specific response that remembers past infections. Understanding how they work explains why we rarely catch measles twice, why vaccines protect us and why diseases that attack immune cells, such as HIV, are so dangerous.

## Key ideas

### Self, non-self and antigens

The immune system must distinguish **self** (the body's own molecules) from **non-self** (foreign molecules). An **antigen** is any molecule that can be specifically recognised by the adaptive immune system, typically a protein or polysaccharide on a pathogen surface. The small part of an antigen that a receptor actually binds is an **epitope**; one antigen can carry many epitopes.

### Innate immunity

**Innate immunity** is present from birth, responds within minutes to hours, and recognises broad groups of pathogens rather than specific ones. It does not improve with repeated exposure.

Innate cells carry **pattern recognition receptors**, such as **Toll-like receptors** (TLRs), which bind molecules common to many microbes but absent from host cells, such as bacterial lipopolysaccharide, flagellin or viral double-stranded RNA.

Components include:

- **Barriers** — skin, mucous membranes, cilia, stomach acid, lysozyme.
- **Phagocytes** — **neutrophils** (the most abundant white blood cells, first to arrive at infection) and **macrophages** (long-lived cells that engulf pathogens and debris). **Phagocytosis** is the engulfing of particles into a vesicle that fuses with a lysosome, where enzymes destroy them.
- **Dendritic cells** — phagocytes that capture antigens and carry them to lymph nodes; they link innate and adaptive immunity.
- **Natural killer (NK) cells** — kill virus-infected and cancer cells that show abnormal surface molecules, such as reduced MHC class I.
- **Antimicrobial proteins** — **interferons** (released by virus-infected cells, they warn neighbouring cells to resist viral replication) and the **complement system** (blood proteins that coat pathogens, attract phagocytes and can punch holes in microbial membranes).
- **Inflammation** — damaged tissue and immune cells release signals such as **histamine** that dilate blood vessels and make them leakier. This produces redness, heat, swelling and pain, and lets phagocytes and proteins reach the site. **Fever** is a whole-body response that can slow some pathogens and speed up immune activity.

### Adaptive immunity

**Adaptive immunity** is found in vertebrates. It is slower on first exposure (days), highly specific to particular epitopes, and produces **immunological memory**, so later responses are faster and stronger. It is carried out by **lymphocytes**: **B cells** (mature in the bone marrow) and **T cells** (mature in the thymus).

Each lymphocyte carries many copies of one type of antigen receptor. During development, gene segments are randomly rearranged, so different lymphocytes have different receptors, creating an enormous repertoire able to recognise millions of possible epitopes before ever meeting them. Lymphocytes whose receptors bind strongly to self molecules are mostly eliminated or inactivated during development, producing **self-tolerance**; failure of this process can lead to **autoimmune disease**.

### Clonal selection

When a lymphocyte's receptor binds its matching antigen (and receives the right signals), that cell is "selected" and divides repeatedly. This is **clonal selection**: the cell forms a **clone** of identical cells, all specific for that antigen. The clone produces:

- **Effector cells** — short-lived cells that fight the current infection (plasma cells from B cells; helper and cytotoxic T cells).
- **Memory cells** — long-lived cells that remain after the infection and respond rapidly if the same antigen is met again.

### Antigen presentation and MHC

T cells cannot recognise free antigens. They recognise antigen fragments displayed on cell surfaces by **major histocompatibility complex** (MHC) molecules. This is **antigen presentation**.

- **MHC class I** molecules are found on almost all nucleated cells. They display fragments of proteins made inside the cell. If a cell is infected by a virus or is cancerous, it displays foreign or abnormal peptides, which are recognised by **cytotoxic T cells** (CD8⁺).
- **MHC class II** molecules are found mainly on **antigen-presenting cells** (dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells). These cells engulf pathogens, break them down and display fragments on class II MHC, which are recognised by **helper T cells** (CD4⁺).

Dendritic cells are the most important cells for activating naive T cells; they travel from the infection site to lymph nodes, where many T cells pass by.

### Helper T cells, cytotoxic T cells and B cells

**Helper T cells** are central to adaptive immunity. When activated by an antigen-presenting cell, they release **cytokines** (signalling proteins) that stimulate both B cells and cytotoxic T cells. Without helper T cells, both branches of the adaptive response are severely weakened, which is why HIV infection, which destroys CD4⁺ helper T cells, leads to immunodeficiency.

Adaptive immunity has two arms:

- **Cell-mediated immunity** — **cytotoxic T cells** recognise infected or cancer cells through MHC class I and kill them by releasing **perforin** (which forms pores in the target membrane) and enzymes that trigger **apoptosis** (programmed cell death). This targets pathogens hidden inside cells.
- **Humoral immunity** — **B cells** bind antigens with their membrane-bound antibodies, take them in, and present fragments on MHC class II. A helper T cell specific for the same antigen activates the B cell, which then divides and differentiates into **plasma cells** that secrete large amounts of antibodies, and memory B cells. This targets pathogens and toxins in body fluids.

### Antibodies

An **antibody** (immunoglobulin) is a Y-shaped protein made of two identical **heavy chains** and two identical **light chains** joined by disulfide bonds. The tips of the arms are **variable regions** that form two identical antigen-binding sites; the stem is the **constant region**, which determines the antibody class and how it interacts with other immune components.

Antibodies do not kill pathogens directly. They act by:

- **Neutralisation** — binding to and blocking the parts of viruses or toxins that attach to host cells.
- **Opsonisation** — coating pathogens so phagocytes recognise and engulf them more readily.
- **Agglutination** — cross-linking pathogens into clumps, since each antibody has two binding sites.
- **Complement activation** — triggering complement proteins that can lyse the pathogen.

The main classes include IgM (first produced in a primary response), IgG (most abundant in blood, dominant in secondary responses and able to cross the placenta), IgA (in secretions such as saliva and breast milk) and IgE (involved in allergy and defence against parasitic worms).

### Immunological memory

The **primary immune response** occurs on first exposure to an antigen. It has a lag of several days while the right lymphocytes are selected and expanded, and antibody levels peak at about 10–17 days. The **secondary immune response** occurs on later exposure. Because memory cells are already numerous and ready, it starts within a few days, rises faster, reaches much higher antibody levels, lasts longer and involves antibodies that bind antigen more tightly. Often the pathogen is eliminated before symptoms appear.

### Active and passive immunity, and vaccination

- **Active immunity** — the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells, after infection (natural) or vaccination (artificial). It is long-lasting.
- **Passive immunity** — antibodies are received from another source, such as across the placenta or in breast milk (natural), or by injection of antibodies, such as antivenom (artificial). It acts immediately but is short-lived because no memory cells are made.

A **vaccine** contains antigens from a pathogen, in a form that cannot cause disease, to stimulate a primary response and the formation of memory cells. Types include:

- Live attenuated (weakened) pathogens.
- Inactivated (killed) pathogens.
- Subunit vaccines containing purified proteins or polysaccharides.
- Toxoids — inactivated toxins (tetanus).
- Nucleic acid vaccines, such as mRNA vaccines, which supply instructions for host cells to make a pathogen protein.

Booster doses trigger secondary responses that increase memory cell numbers. When enough of a population is immune, the chain of transmission is broken, protecting those who cannot be vaccinated; this is **herd immunity**.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: interpreting a primary and secondary response

A rabbit is injected with antigen X on day 0 and with antigens X and Y on day 30. Antibody concentration (arbitrary units) is measured.

| Day | Anti-X | Anti-Y |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 5 | 2 | 0 |
| 14 | 20 | 0 |
| 28 | 5 | 0 |
| 35 | 300 | 2 |
| 44 | 450 | 20 |

Step 1 — primary response to X: lag of about 5 days, peak around 20 units at day 14, then decline.

Step 2 — response to X after day 30: within 5 days anti-X reaches 300 units, and by day 44 it is 450, over 20 times the primary peak. This is a secondary response due to memory B cells.

Step 3 — response to Y: identical in shape and size to the first anti-X response. This is a primary response, showing that memory is specific to X.

Step 4 — conclusion: the experiment demonstrates both specificity and memory of adaptive immunity.

### Example 2: predicting effects of losing a cell type

A patient's helper T cell count falls severely. Predict the effects.

- Helper T cells activate B cells, so production of antibodies against most protein antigens falls (humoral immunity is weakened).
- Helper T cells help activate cytotoxic T cells, so killing of virus-infected and cancer cells is reduced (cell-mediated immunity is weakened).
- Innate defences (barriers, neutrophils, complement) still work, but without adaptive support the patient becomes vulnerable to opportunistic infections that a healthy immune system would control.
- This explains the clinical course of untreated HIV infection.

## Common mistakes

- Saying antibodies kill pathogens. They mark, block or clump them; other components do the killing.
- Thinking the antigen causes a lymphocyte to create a matching receptor. Receptors exist before exposure; the antigen selects cells that already carry them.
- Mixing up MHC classes. Class I is on almost all nucleated cells and is read by cytotoxic (CD8⁺) T cells; class II is on antigen-presenting cells and is read by helper (CD4⁺) T cells.
- Calling antivenom or breast milk antibodies "long-lasting immunity". Passive immunity provides no memory.
- Assuming innate immunity is only barriers. It includes many cells and proteins, and it activates adaptive immunity.

## Exam tips

- For primary versus secondary response graphs, compare lag time, peak concentration and duration, quoting values from the graph.
- Describe the steps from antigen entry to antibody production in order: antigen presentation, helper T cell activation, B cell activation, clonal expansion, plasma and memory cells.
- Use precise cell names (cytotoxic T cell, plasma cell) rather than "white blood cell".
- Explain vaccination by linking it to memory cells and the secondary response.

## Tips to remember

- **The "rule of 8"**: multiply the MHC class by the CD number and you always get 8. MHC class I × CD8 (cytotoxic T cells) = 8; MHC class II × CD4 (helper T cells) = 8.
- **Innate is the security guard, adaptive is the detective with a filing cabinet**: the guard responds within minutes to anything suspicious but never learns; the detective takes days on a new case, targets one specific culprit and keeps a file (memory cells) for next time.
- **Clonal selection is a shop picking from stock, not tailoring to order**: every lymphocyte's receptor already exists before infection. The antigen simply "selects" the matching cell, which then copies itself into effector cells and memory cells.
- **What antibodies do: "NOAC"** (made-up memory trick): **N**eutralisation, **O**psonisation, **A**gglutination, **C**omplement activation. Notice none of them is "kill directly".
- **Antibody classes by letter** (made-up memory trick): Ig**M** = **M**akes the first move in a primary response; Ig**G** = most abundant, crosses the placenta during **G**estation; Ig**A** = in secretions such as saliva and breast milk; Ig**E** = "**E**ek!", allergy and defence against parasitic worms.
- **Active = you make it, it lasts; passive = you're lent it, it fades**: vaccines and infection give memory cells; breast milk, placental antibodies and antivenom act immediately but leave no memory.

## Key terms

- **Antigen** — a molecule recognised specifically by the adaptive immune system.
- **Epitope** — the part of an antigen bound by a receptor or antibody.
- **Pattern recognition receptor** — an innate receptor that binds molecules common to microbes.
- **Clonal selection** — antigen-driven proliferation of the lymphocytes that carry matching receptors.
- **MHC** — cell-surface molecules that present peptide fragments to T cells.
- **Antigen-presenting cell** — a cell (dendritic cell, macrophage, B cell) that displays antigens on MHC class II.
- **Helper T cell** — CD4⁺ cell that releases cytokines to activate B and cytotoxic T cells.
- **Cytotoxic T cell** — CD8⁺ cell that kills infected or cancerous cells.
- **Plasma cell** — an effector B cell that secretes antibodies.
- **Vaccine** — a preparation of antigens that induces active immunity and memory.

## Summary

- Innate immunity is rapid and general, using barriers, phagocytes, NK cells, complement, interferons and inflammation.
- Adaptive immunity is specific and has memory, carried out by B and T lymphocytes selected by antigen.
- MHC class I presents internal antigens to cytotoxic T cells; MHC class II presents engulfed antigens to helper T cells.
- Antibodies neutralise, opsonise, agglutinate and activate complement.
- Memory cells make secondary responses faster and stronger.
- Vaccines produce active immunity and, at high coverage, herd immunity.

questions.prompt: Which cells secrete large quantities of antibodies during an immune response?
questions.explanation: Plasma cells are effector B cells specialised for antibody secretion. Memory B cells (C) are tempting, but they are long-lived cells that wait for later exposure rather than secreting large amounts of antibody.

questions.prompt: MHC class I molecules are found on:

options.A: Almost all nucleated cells, presenting peptides from proteins made inside the cell
options.B: Only antigen-presenting cells, presenting fragments of engulfed pathogens
options.D: Only B cells, as membrane-bound antibodies

questions.explanation: Class I is displayed by nearly all nucleated cells, allowing cytotoxic T cells to check for infection or cancer. B describes MHC class II, the most common mix-up.

questions.prompt: According to the clonal selection model, why does only a tiny fraction of B cells respond to a particular pathogen?

options.A: The pathogen causes all B cells to make matching receptors, but only some succeed
options.B: Most B cells are destroyed by the pathogen
options.C: Only B cells already carrying receptors that bind the pathogen's epitopes are selected to divide
options.D: B cells respond only after innate immunity has completely cleared the infection

questions.explanation: Receptor diversity is generated randomly before exposure, and antigen selects the few cells with matching receptors. A is the instructive misconception that antigens tell cells what receptor to make.

questions.prompt: Why does destruction of helper T cells by HIV weaken both humoral and cell-mediated immunity?

options.A: Helper T cells are the cells that produce antibodies
options.B: Helper T cells release cytokines needed to activate both B cells and cytotoxic T cells
options.C: Helper T cells are the only cells that recognise MHC class I
options.D: Helper T cells are the main phagocytes in the blood

questions.explanation: Helper T cells coordinate both arms via cytokines; without them, B cell and cytotoxic T cell activation fails. A is wrong because plasma cells, not helper T cells, make antibodies.

questions.prompt: A snakebite victim is given antivenom containing antibodies against the venom. Which statement is correct?

options.A: It gives active immunity that will protect against future bites
options.B: It stimulates memory cells so the victim responds faster next time
options.C: It acts slowly because the body must first make plasma cells
options.D: It gives artificial passive immunity that acts immediately but does not produce memory

questions.explanation: Ready-made antibodies act at once but are broken down within weeks and no memory cells form. A and B are tempting because injections are linked to vaccines, but antivenom supplies antibodies rather than antigens.

questions.prompt: A virus-infected cell displays viral peptides on MHC class I. Which response most directly destroys this cell?

options.A: Cytotoxic T cells releasing perforin and inducing apoptosis
options.B: Antibodies neutralising the virus inside the cell
options.C: Helper T cells engulfing the infected cell

questions.explanation: Cytotoxic T cells recognise peptide on MHC class I and kill the target cell. B is wrong because antibodies act outside cells and cannot reach virus replicating inside.

questions.prompt: Anti-X antibody peaked at 20 units after a first injection of antigen X and at 450 units after a second injection. Antigen Y, injected for the first time with the second dose of X, produced a peak of 20 units. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.A: Antigen Y suppresses the response to X
options.B: The second response to X is about 22 times greater because of memory cells, and memory is specific to X
options.C: The second injection of X contained more antigen, so the response is not due to memory
options.D: Memory cells for X also respond strongly to Y

questions.explanation: 450/20 ≈ 22, a typical secondary response, while Y gave only a primary-sized response, showing specificity. D contradicts the data, since anti-Y was no larger than a first response.

questions.prompt: Why do booster doses of a vaccine improve long-term protection?

options.A: They provide passive antibodies that last for life
options.B: They replace the innate immune system
options.C: They trigger a secondary response that further increases the number of memory cells and antibody levels
options.D: They stop the body from making IgM

questions.explanation: Re-exposure to vaccine antigen activates memory cells, expanding the memory population and raising antibody levels. A is wrong because vaccines give active immunity; they do not provide antibodies directly.
